gloss: To make someone or something remembered forever, especially in art, writing, or film.
examples: Photographers *immortalize* moments that would otherwise be forgotten.
The song *immortalized* a small town in Kansas.
Her face has been *immortalized* on the ten-dollar bill.
contrast: American spelling is *immortalize*; British writing uses *immortalise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the cuts impacted every department*), intransitive (*the meteor impacted at enormous speed*)
gloss: To have a strong effect on someone or something.
examples: Rising fuel prices *impact* every part of the economy.
The strike *impacted* deliveries for three weeks.
Sales have been badly *impacted* by the recall.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, IM-pact; the verb on the second, im-PACT.

gloss: To pierce something right through with a sharp, pointed object.
examples: Do not *impale* the steak with a fork, or the juices run out.
A branch *impaled* the tire and the car skidded off the road.
Receipts were *impaled* on a metal spike beside the register.

gloss: To drive someone to act, usually because of a strong feeling or need.
examples: Curiosity *impels* scientists to ask uncomfortable questions.
Something *impelled* her to open the letter right away.
He felt *impelled* to speak up at the meeting.
contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable, so the l doubles: *impelled*, *impelling*.

gloss: To put someone or something in danger.
examples: New tariffs could *imperil* thousands of jobs.
The leak *imperiled* the whole investigation.
Several species are *imperiled* by the loss of wetlands.
contrast: American English keeps one l: *imperiled*, *imperiling*. British English doubles it: *imperilled*.

gloss: To have an effect on something, especially by intruding on it or limiting it.
examples: The new rules *impinge* on the rights of tenants.
Work *impinged* on every weekend that spring.
She felt her privacy was being *impinged* upon.
contrast: Always takes *on* or *upon*: *impinge on your freedom*, never *impinge your freedom*.

gloss: To put something into a body or into someone's mind so that it stays there.
examples: Surgeons *implant* a small device just under the collarbone.
The ad campaign *implanted* the slogan in everyone's head.
A chip had been *implanted* under the dog's skin.
contrast: The noun is IM-plant (the device); the verb is im-PLANT (the action).

transitivity: both — transitive (*crews imploded the old stadium*), intransitive (*the company imploded*)
gloss: To collapse violently inward, or to fail suddenly and completely.
examples: Crews will *implode* the old hotel on Sunday morning.
The startup *imploded* after its funding fell through.
The tank had *imploded* under the pressure of the water.
contrast: The opposite of *explode*: an implosion collapses inward rather than blowing outward.

gloss: To beg someone earnestly to do something.
examples: I *implore* you to think it over before you sign anything.
She *implored* the judge for more time.
They had *implored* him not to drive in that weather.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the city imposed a curfew*), intransitive (*I hope I am not imposing*)
gloss: To force a rule, tax, or opinion on someone, or to take unfair advantage of someone's kindness.
examples: The state may *impose* a fine of up to a thousand dollars.
They *imposed* strict limits on water use.
Sanctions have been *imposed* on three more banks.
contrast: Takes *on*: *impose a tax on imports*; *I do not want to impose on you*.

gloss: To make a person, place, or thing poor or much weaker.
examples: A long war can *impoverish* a country for a generation.
The closing of the mine *impoverished* the entire valley.
Soil that has been *impoverished* by overfarming grows almost nothing.

gloss: To soak something thoroughly with a substance, or to make a female pregnant.
examples: They *impregnate* the wood with a preservative before shipping it.
The rain *impregnated* the canvas with a musty smell.
The paper is *impregnated* with a chemical that turns blue in acid.

gloss: To attack something as false, especially someone's honesty or motives.
examples: No one here is trying to *impugn* your integrity.
The defense *impugned* the witness's memory of that night.
His motives have been *impugned* in every editorial this week.
contrast: The g is silent: im-PYOON, rhyming with *soon*.

gloss: To say that someone or something is responsible for an action or quality, often unfairly.
examples: Do not *impute* motives to people you have never met.
The report *imputed* the delay to poor planning.
Income *imputed* from the rental has to be declared.
contrast: Takes *to*: you *impute* something *to* someone.

gloss: To make someone or something unable to work or function normally.
examples: A single blow to the knee can *incapacitate* a runner for months.
The flu *incapacitated* half the office in one week.
He was *incapacitated* by the injury and could not testify.

gloss: To make someone extremely angry.
examples: Remarks like that *incense* the people who did the actual work.
The decision *incensed* fans across the country.
Parents were *incensed* by the sudden change to the schedule.
contrast: The noun (the fragrant smoke) is IN-sens; the verb is in-SENS.

gloss: To give someone a reward or advantage that encourages them to act in a particular way.
examples: Tax credits *incentivize* companies to hire locally.
The city *incentivized* builders with cheaper permits.
Recycling has been *incentivized* through a deposit on every bottle.
contrast: American spelling is *incentivize*; British writing uses *incentivise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*he inched the car forward*), intransitive (*traffic inched along*)
gloss: To move very slowly, a little at a time.
examples: Just *inch* the couch to the left a few more feet.
The line *inched* forward for two hours.
Prices have been *inching* up since January.

gloss: To destroy something completely by burning it.
examples: The plant *incinerates* about two hundred tons of trash a day.
The fire *incinerated* everything in the storage unit.
Medical waste must be *incinerated*, not buried.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the evidence inclines me to agree*), intransitive (*the roof inclines steeply*)
gloss: To slope or lean, or to make someone tend toward a particular opinion or action.
examples: The ramp *inclines* gently toward the entrance.
Her calm tone *inclined* us to believe her.
I am *inclined* to wait another week before deciding.
contrast: The noun is IN-cline (a slope); the verb is in-CLINE.

gloss: To cause someone trouble or difficulty.
examples: I hope the change does not *inconvenience* you too much.
The detour *inconvenienced* thousands of commuters.
Passengers *inconvenienced* by the delay were offered vouchers.
contrast: The silent e stays before -ing so the c keeps its soft sound: *inconveniencing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*incorporate the feedback*), intransitive (*the firm incorporated in Delaware*)
gloss: To include something as part of a larger whole, or to form a legal corporation.
examples: Try to *incorporate* the reviewers' comments into the draft.
They *incorporated* the business in Nevada for tax reasons.
Several of her ideas were *incorporated* into the final design.

gloss: To increase a number or value by a fixed amount, usually by one.
examples: The loop *increments* the counter on every pass.
We *incremented* the version number before the release.
The build number is *incremented* automatically.

gloss: To fix an idea or habit in someone's mind by repeating it often.
examples: Coaches try to *inculcate* discipline from the very first practice.
Her parents *inculcated* a love of reading early on.
Those values had been *inculcated* in him since childhood.

gloss: To bring something unpleasant, especially a cost or a penalty, on yourself by your own actions.
examples: Late payments *incur* a fee of twenty dollars.
The team *incurred* heavy losses in the first quarter.
Any debt *incurred* before the marriage stays separate.
contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable, so the r doubles: *incurred*, *incurring*.

gloss: To promise to pay someone back for any loss or damage they suffer.
examples: The contract requires the vendor to *indemnify* the city.
The insurer *indemnified* the family for the whole loss.
Volunteers are *indemnified* against claims arising from the event.
contrast: The y becomes i before -es and -ed (*indemnifies*, *indemnified*) but stays before -ing (*indemnifying*).

gloss: To formally charge someone with a serious crime.
examples: A grand jury can *indict* on far less evidence than a trial requires.
Prosecutors *indicted* four executives last spring.
He was *indicted* on charges of fraud.
contrast: The c is silent: in-DYT, rhyming with *night*, not with *strict*.

gloss: To adapt something so that it suits one particular person.
examples: Good teachers *individualize* the work for each student.
The clinic *individualized* her treatment after the second visit.
Every lesson plan here is *individualized*.
contrast: American spelling is *individualize*; British writing uses *individualise*.

gloss: To teach someone a set of beliefs so thoroughly that they accept them without question.
examples: Regimes *indoctrinate* children through the school system.
The group *indoctrinated* new members over several months.
He claimed he had been *indoctrinated* as a teenager.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the state industrialized the north*), intransitive (*the region industrialized quickly*)
gloss: To develop factories and industry in a country or region on a large scale.
examples: Cheap energy helped the region *industrialize*.
Japan *industrialized* at remarkable speed.
Much of the coastline has been heavily *industrialized*.
contrast: American spelling is *industrialize*; British writing uses *industrialise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*agents infiltrated the group*), intransitive (*water infiltrates into the soil*)
gloss: To enter a place or organization secretly, usually to gather information or cause harm.
examples: It took two years to *infiltrate* the smuggling ring.
An undercover officer *infiltrated* the meeting.
The network had been *infiltrated* months earlier.

gloss: To make a feeling, a conflict, or a part of the body worse and more painful or intense.
examples: Careless remarks can *inflame* an already tense situation.
The verdict *inflamed* protests across the city.
His knee was badly *inflamed* after the game.

ru: склонять, спрягать (изменять форму слова); менять интонацию
transitivity: both — transitive (*English inflects verbs for tense*), intransitive (*these nouns do not inflect*)
gloss: To change the form of a word to show tense, number, or case, or to change the pitch of your voice.
examples: Russian *inflects* nouns for six cases.
She *inflected* the last word so that it sounded like a question.
Most English adjectives are not *inflected* at all.

gloss: To cause someone to suffer something unpleasant, such as pain, damage, or a punishment.
examples: I would not *inflict* that movie on my worst enemy.
The storm *inflicted* millions of dollars in damage.
The wounds were *inflicted* with a blunt object.
contrast: You inflict something *on* someone: *inflict pain on a rival*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the design infringes two patents*), intransitive (*it infringes on his rights*)
gloss: To break a law or agreement, or to limit someone's rights unfairly.
examples: The design *infringes* two of our patents.
The company *infringed* on a trademark it had never heard of.
No right may be *infringed* without due process.
contrast: Transitive with a patent or copyright, but *on* or *upon* with a right or freedom.

transitivity: both — transitive (*infuse the oil with garlic*), intransitive (*let the tea infuse*)
gloss: To fill something with a quality or substance, or to soak something in liquid to draw out its flavor.
examples: A good director can *infuse* a tired script with real energy.
She *infused* the vinegar with chili peppers.
The cake was *infused* with lemon.

gloss: To take food, drink, or another substance into the body, usually by swallowing.
examples: Children can *ingest* lead from old paint chips.
The dog *ingested* something toxic in the yard.
The amount *ingested* was too small to cause harm.

gloss: To fix a habit, belief, or attitude so firmly in someone that it becomes very hard to change.
examples: Years of drills *ingrain* the motion until you stop thinking about it.
The training *ingrained* a habit of checking everything twice.
Those attitudes are deeply *ingrained* in the culture.

gloss: To try to make someone like you, usually by flattering them or doing them favors.
examples: He will do anything to *ingratiate* himself with the boss.
She *ingratiated* herself with the neighbors by shoveling their walk.
He spent the evening *ingratiating* himself with the investors.
contrast: Always reflexive and followed by *with*: *ingratiate yourself with someone*.

gloss: To live in a particular place.
examples: Only a few hundred people *inhabit* the island year-round.
Wolves once *inhabited* most of the state.
The cabin has not been *inhabited* since the fire.
contrast: The last syllable is unstressed, so the t does not double: *inhabited*, not *inhabitted* (compare *admit* to *admitted*).

gloss: To slow down or prevent a process, or to make someone feel unable to act freely.
examples: Cold weather *inhibits* the growth of the seedlings.
The camera *inhibited* everyone at the table.
Recovery was *inhibited* by a lack of sleep.
contrast: The stress is on HIB, so the final t stays single: *inhibited*, *inhibiting*.

gloss: To set something, especially a computer variable or a device, to its starting state.
examples: You have to *initialize* the array before you use it.
The script *initialized* the database with default settings.
The drive must be *initialized* before it will mount.
contrast: American spelling is *initialize*; British writing uses *initialise*.

gloss: To sign a contract or agreement, a use common in American sports and business reporting.
examples: The team hopes to *ink* a deal before the deadline.
She *inked* a two-year extension last month.
The agreement was *inked* in Geneva on Friday.

gloss: To suggest something unpleasant indirectly rather than saying it openly.
examples: Are you trying to *insinuate* that I lied?
He *insinuated* that the results had been arranged in advance.
Nothing was said directly, but a great deal was *insinuated*.

gloss: To create an actual instance of something general, especially an object from a class in programming.
examples: The factory method *instantiates* the right handler for each file type.
We *instantiated* the client once and reused it everywhere.
A new session is *instantiated* for every request.

gloss: To bury a dead body, especially in a formal ceremony.
examples: The family chose to *inter* the ashes beside her parents.
They *interred* him with full military honors.
Hundreds of soldiers are *interred* in that cemetery.
contrast: The r doubles: *interred*, *interring*. Do not confuse it with *intern*, which means to detain someone.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the cable interconnects the buildings*), intransitive (*the tunnels interconnect*)
gloss: To connect two or more things to each other so that they work together.
examples: Fiber lines *interconnect* all the campus buildings.
Engineers *interconnected* the two power grids last year.
Everything in the ecosystem is *interconnected*.

gloss: To work together or communicate with another person, system, or device.
examples: The scanner *interfaces* with any standard laptop.
Our team *interfaced* directly with the client's engineers.
The two systems have never *interfaced* well.
contrast: Takes *with*: *interface with the payroll system*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*interlock your fingers*), intransitive (*the pieces interlock*)
gloss: To fit two or more things together so that they hold each other in place.
examples: The bricks *interlock* without any mortar at all.
She *interlocked* her fingers and waited.
The panels are *interlocked* along every edge.

ru: заключать смешанные браки, вступать в брак между собой
gloss: To marry someone from a different group, religion, or family.
examples: The two communities began to *intermarry* in the 1920s.
Settlers *intermarried* with the people already living there.
Their families had *intermarried* for generations.
contrast: The y becomes i before -es and -ed (*intermarries*, *intermarried*) but stays before -ing (*intermarrying*).

transitivity: both — transitive (*they intermingled the two flocks*), intransitive (*the crowds intermingled*)
gloss: To mix together, or to mix things together, so that they are no longer separate.
examples: Guests from both parties began to *intermingle* around the bar.
Smoke *intermingled* with the fog over the river.
The two styles are thoroughly *intermingled* in her later work.

gloss: To estimate a value that lies between two known values, or to insert something into a text.
examples: The software will *interpolate* the missing readings.
A later editor *interpolated* two lines into the poem.
Temperatures between stations are *interpolated* from the nearest sensors.

gloss: To be connected to each other in a way that makes each one affect the other.
examples: The chapters *interrelate* more closely than they first appear to.
The study showed how sleep and mood *interrelated*.
Climate, soil, and crop yield are closely *interrelated*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the highway intersects the river*), intransitive (*the two lines intersect*)
gloss: To cross another line, road, or area, or to meet and cross each other.
examples: The two trails *intersect* just past the bridge.
A fire road *intersected* the path at the ridge.
Their careers have *intersected* several times.

gloss: To scatter things here and there among other things.
examples: *Intersperse* the photographs through the text instead of grouping them.
He *interspersed* the lecture with jokes.
The lawn is *interspersed* with wildflowers.
contrast: Usually used with *with*: *interspersed with quotations*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*she intertwined the ribbons*), intransitive (*the vines intertwine*)
gloss: To twist together, or to connect two things so closely that they cannot be separated.
examples: The vines *intertwine* along the whole length of the fence.
History *intertwined* the two families long before the wedding.
Their finances are hopelessly *intertwined*.

gloss: To suggest or hint at something rather than say it directly.
examples: He would not *intimate* how the vote might go.
She *intimated* that she might resign in the spring.
It had been *intimated* to us that the funding was at risk.
contrast: The adjective (*an intimate dinner*) ends in -muht; the verb ends in -mayt: IN-tuh-mayt.

gloss: To make someone drunk, or to excite someone so much that they cannot think clearly.
examples: Two drinks are enough to *intoxicate* someone that size.
Early success *intoxicated* the young band.
He was arrested for driving while *intoxicated*.

gloss: To put a tube into a person's windpipe so that they can breathe.
examples: Paramedics may have to *intubate* at the scene.
Doctors *intubated* her within minutes of her arrival.
He spent nine days *intubated* in intensive care.

gloss: To understand or know something by feeling rather than by reasoning or evidence.
examples: Good salespeople *intuit* what a customer actually wants.
She *intuited* right away that something was wrong.
The answer had been *intuited* long before anyone could prove it.

gloss: To make someone so used to something unpleasant that it no longer bothers them.
examples: Years on the night shift *inure* you to the noise.
The work *inured* her to the sight of blood.
Residents have become *inured* to the sirens.
contrast: Almost always passive and followed by *to*: *be inured to hardship*.

gloss: To make a complete list of the goods or items in a place.
examples: Volunteers *inventory* the food pantry every Monday.
The staff *inventoried* everything in the warehouse.
All the equipment has been *inventoried* and tagged.
contrast: The y becomes i before -es and -ed (*inventories*, *inventoried*) but stays before -ing (*inventorying*).

ru: переворачивать, перевернуть; менять порядок на обратный
gloss: To turn something upside down or reverse its order or position.
examples: *Invert* the pan over a plate and lift it straight off.
The question *inverted* the usual order of subject and verb.
The image is *inverted* by the lens.

gloss: To give someone or something new energy and strength.
examples: A cold swim will *invigorate* you faster than coffee.
New leadership *invigorated* the whole department.
She came back from the trip looking *invigorated*.
